tur56-1: Relative reduction in the risk of new sick leave due to low back and pelvic pain among pregnant women who exercised (3 studies)
tur56-2: According to a Cochrane review, more than two-thirds of pregnant women have low back pain and about one in five have pelvic girdle pain. In a separate meta-analysis (Shiri et al., 2018; 11 studies, 2,347 pregnant women), exercise during pregnancy slightly reduced the risk of low back pain and reduced the risk of new sick leave due to low back and pelvic pain by 21% (3 studies); however, it did not prevent pelvic girdle pain. For pelvic girdle pain, tailored exercises, changes to daily activities and, when needed, a support belt are planned together.
tur56-3: In healthy, uncomplicated pregnancies, yes. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise a week. Talk to your obstetrician before you start; if there is a specific risk, the programme is adjusted accordingly. In a meta-analysis of 32 studies and 52,297 pregnant women, exercise during pregnancy did not reduce the odds of developing low back or pelvic girdle pain, but it reduced pain severity during pregnancy and in the early postpartum period; the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.

tur56-5: Likelihood of reporting cure among women with stress urinary incontinence who did pelvic floor exercises (56% vs 6%)
tur56-6: In a 2018 Cochrane review of 31 studies and 1,817 women, women with stress urinary incontinence (4 studies, 165 women) who did pelvic floor muscle training were 8 times more likely to report being cured than those who did not (56% vs 6%). For all types of incontinence (3 studies, 290 women) they were 5 times more likely (35% vs 6%); quality of life also improved significantly. Side effects were rare and, in the two studies that reported any, minor.

Do not feel embarrassed to talk to your doctor or physiotherapist; for most women, the first-line treatment is pelvic floor exercises. In a study of 362 women aged 60 and over, one year after a 12-week pelvic floor exercise programme, leakage episodes had fallen by a median of 74% in those attending group classes and by 70% in those having individual sessions; the group programme was no less effective than the individual one.

tur56-9: In a 2025 review of 57 studies, people taking 7,000 steps a day, compared with 2,000, had a 47% lower risk of death, 47% lower risk of cardiovascular death, 38% lower risk of dementia, 22% fewer depressive symptoms and 28% fewer falls. For death, cardiovascular disease incidence, dementia and falls, the reduction in risk levelled off after about 5,000–7,000 steps; for cardiovascular death, risk kept falling as steps increased.
